You are a senior credit analyst building a notebook of every fact that matters for deciding whether to grant a credit line to a borrower. You read a borrower's document pack one window at a time.

Write only facts that bear on the credit decision: repayment capacity, leverage, liquidity, cash flow, ratings, defaults, litigation and regulatory actions, auditor remarks, promoter holding and pledge, concentration, and the figures in the checklist below. Do not write boilerplate (meeting notices, e-voting and proxy mechanics), governance trivia (committee membership, attendance, meeting counts, policy lists), CSR and ESG programmes, awards, product marketing or generic industry narrative; when unsure whether a fact can change the decision, leave it out. Cover these categories exactly:
revenue, profitability, debt_leverage, liquidity, cash_flow, credit_history, ratings, stock,
ownership_governance, litigation_regulatory, industry_market, news, other.

Classify each entry's kind as one of:
- fact: a qualitative statement about the business, owners, or events.
- number: a figure, ratio, amount, date, or other measured quantity.
- concern: a risk, weakness, breach, or open question a credit officer should notice.

Give importance on this scale, and be stingy:
1 = boilerplate.
2 = minor detail.
3 = useful context (the default; most entries).
4 = only for a topic the bank's credit policy names: external ratings and outlook, litigation,
    auditor remarks or qualifications, promoter holding and pledge, regulatory actions
    (inspections, warning letters, penalties), defaults and overdue payments, and caution-list
    sectors (customer or supplier concentration, stressed sectors).
Never give 5: the program raises the facts that feed the bank's rules and scores itself.
Rate 4 only when the entry is about one of those topics; at most a fifth of your entries.

Rules:
- Cite only chunk ids that appear in the new chunks shown to you, in square brackets,
  such as D1:p12:c3. Never invent a chunk id.
- Prefer numbers with their period and unit (for example "Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in
  FY25"), and keep restatements separate when the period or basis changes.
- If a new entry restates or replaces an earlier notebook entry, set supersedes to that
  earlier entry's id.
- Write each statement as one self-contained sentence that can be verified against the
  cited chunks. Do not speculate beyond the document.
- Stay literal. Do not add comparisons ("exceeding", "higher than", "in line with"), causal
  qualifiers ("due to", "because", "driven by") or evaluations unless those exact words are in
  the cited text. Keep the text's own subject: never swap it for a related one (a "warning
  letter" is not an "OAI status"; a subsidiary is not the group).
- Always record rating actions, the outlook and its rationale, upgrade and downgrade triggers
  ("rating may be downgraded if ..."), and each rating-history row (as "rating was X on <date>;
  Y on <date>"), even if they repeat what an earlier document already said.
- Use the source's own metric names: never rename revenue as operating income or operating
  income as revenue, and never swap one metric for a related one.
- Every entry must carry at least one chunk id from the new chunks. Never omit the chunk id.
- Never write meta-commentary about the document or the passages ("the passages do not
  mention...", "no information is available"). If a window has nothing to record, return
  no entries.
- Return only the new entries for this window, not the entries already in the notebook.

Reply format: minified JSON on one line, no indentation, no Markdown fences, using the short keys of the schema (s statement, c chunk_ids, cat category, k kind, i importance, sup supersedes; for records m metric, v value, u unit, p period, sc scope, q qualifier, pv previous_value, pp previous_period). Omit keys whose value is the default (empty or null). Example:
{"entries":[{"s":"Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in FY25.","c":["D1:p12:c3"],"cat":"revenue","k":"number","i":4}],"records":[]}

Credit-policy checklist (Demo Bank of India — Corporate and SME Credit Policy (Working Capital and Term Credit)):
- Operating profit before depreciation, interest and tax, excluding other income
- Gross finance cost for the year
- Total borrowings (short and long term, including current maturities and leases)
- Shareholders' equity (net worth) at year end
- Total current assets at year end
- Total current liabilities at year end
- Revenue from operations, latest audited year
- Revenue from operations, previous audited year
- Financial Strength Score computed under policy section 10.1
- Internal Risk Grade computed under policy section 10.2
- Total borrowings less cash, bank balances and liquid investments, latest audited year: write its components (total borrowings, lease liabilities, cash and bank balances, liquid investments)
- Cash flow available for debt service: EBITDA less cash taxes paid: write its components (ebitda, cash taxes paid)
- Interest paid plus scheduled principal repayments in the year: write its components (interest paid, scheduled principal repayments)
- Tangible net worth at year end: write its components (total_equity, intangible assets)
- Rules tested: Net debt / EBITDA at most 4.5x; Interest coverage at least 2.5x; DSCR at least 1.25x; Current ratio at least 1.10x; Total debt / equity at most 3.0x; Revenue trend not below -10%; Tangible net worth positive; External rating at least BBB-; No default flag; Fewer than two major red flags; No major red flag; Proposed exposure within the maximum exposure; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 7; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 5; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 3
- Regulatory actions: warning letters, adverse inspections, licence suspensions, penalties (any regulator)
- External rating grade, outlook, watch status and rating history, the agency's metrics (interest coverage, DSCR) and rationale
- Auditor: qualifications, emphasis of matter, going-concern doubts (also on investees)
- Defaults: delays in repayment, CARO statements on dues, NPA or SMA classification
- Asset sales, monetisation, divestments and acquisitions
- Working capital: intensity, debtor and inventory days
- Latest quarter or half-year results: income, profit, margins
- Red-flag and default evidence: adverse opinion, auditor resign, default, disclaimer, forensic, Form 483, fraud, going concern, IBC, insolvency, litigation, non-performing, NPA, OAI, one-time settlement, OTS, overdue, pledge, promoter loan, qualification, qualified, regulatory proceeding, related party, related-party, resignation, SMA, warning letter, wilful

Rationale
The rating reaffirmation and the continuation of the negative outlook on the long-term rating take into account the deterioration
in Indoco Remedies Limited’s (IRL/ the company) revenues, operating net profit margins and debt metrics in FY2025 and the
company’s continued weak performance in Q1 FY2026. ICRA expects the company’s debt metrics to remain impacted in FY2026
by high debt levels. The company’s performance was weaker-than-expected in FY2025 and Q1 FY2026, primarily due to supply-
side disruptions caused by the ongoing refurbishment of its manufacturing plants as part of its master manufacturing plan (MMP)
and the ongoing remediation for its Goa facility. This impacted its sales to export markets, leading to a contraction in IRL’s
operating margins. Further, the company’s continued investments in the over the counter (OTC)toothpaste segment have also
impacted the margins to a certain extent.
While the company’s total debt has reduced marginally to around Rs. 952 crore as on June 30, 2025 over Rs. 994 crore as on
March 31, 2025, it remains elevated compared to Rs. 672 crore as on March 31, 2024. The increase was primarily driven by the
ongoing capex for refurbishing manufacturing plants in Goa, Waluj (Maharashtra) and Baddi (Himachal Pradesh), additional lines
at Sterile site in Goa and fast-tracked debt-funded capex in its wholly-owned subsidiary, Warren Remedies Limited, to establish
facilities for toothpaste and active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) manufacturing. Overall, the company availed additional debt
of about Rs. 264.3 crore in FY2025. Along with deterioration in operating profit margin (OPM) to 6.0% in FY2025 from 13.4% in
FY2024, this resulted in a deterioration in its debt metrics.
The ratings, however, continue to draw comfort from IRL’s established position in the domestic formulation segment and its
diversified geographic presence.

was postponed due to shipment delays from the original equipment manufacturer (OEM). Revenue from the US also declined

The company’s OPM deteriorated in FY2025 and continued to remain weak in Q1 FY2026 primarily due to expenditure towards
ongoing remediations for the resolution of the OAI status for its Goa Plants II and III, increased employee costs and higher
marketing expenses for the newly launched OTC toothpaste brand. Further, reduction in sales to export markets, which are
usually margin-accretive, also impacted the company’s margins. The margins for FY2026 are expected to improve gradually over
the next few quarters as most of the remediation and upgradation cost are completed and larger batch sizes as part of the
company’s MMP result in better economies of scale. Trajectory and impact of the same on the company’s debt metrics will
remain a key monitorable. ICRA expects the company’s investments in plant and process improvements, which will yield benefits
in the medium-to-long term.
The ratings also factor in IRL’s moderate scale of operations; although the same is expected to scale up, supported by improving
presence in the domestic market, anticipated recovery in its supplies to export markets driven by a robust order book. While the
company has received approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) to commence operations at two of its four
lines, timely resolution of the warning letter remains a key monitorable. ICRA also notes that the Goa facility has recently received
approval from the European authorities.
The company is expected to incur capex of Rs. 50 crore in FY2026 and around Rs. 50–60 crore in FY2027 towards maintenance
capex and addition of new lines at Goa Plant II. The same is expected to be funded through internal accruals and funding which
is already secured. Total debt/OPBDITA for the company increased to 10.0 times as on March 31, 2025 from 2.8 times as on
March 31, 2024. The total interest coverage has also declined to 1.5 times in FY2025 and 0.7 times in Q1 FY2026 from 6.4 times
in FY2024. While ICRA notes that the that the interest costs for Q1 FY2026 included mark-to-market losses of around Rs. 7.4
crore, which are notional in nature, interest cover adjusted for the same still remain below 1.0 times. ICRA expects debt indicators
to improve gradually from FY2026, supported by the scheduled amortisation of term debt and improving cash accruals with a

Key rating drivers and their description
Credit strengths
Experienced management team – At present, the company’s operations are managed by Ms. Aditi Kare Panandikar and
Mr. Sundeep Bambolkar, both of whom have over 30 years of experience in the pharmaceutical industry, supported by a
professional management team.
Established brands in dental, respiratory, gastrointestinal and anti-infective therapies of domestic formulations market –
IRL’s presence in the domestic formulations market is primarily in mature molecules of acute therapies with intense
competition. It has wide therapeutic coverage with a strong presence in anti-infective, respiratory, gastrointestinal, vitamin
and stomatological therapies. The company enjoys a healthy reputation in the domestic market, with its major brands
positioned among the top five of the respective therapy segments. However, given the mature molecules and the large number
of players in the field, IRL’s market share and pricing power remain low. Although the company’s legacy brands in acute
therapies such as respiratory and anti-infectives witnessed a revenue decline in FY2025, the domestic formulation segment
had a revenue growth supported by a healthy performance in therapies such as stomatological, urology, vitamins, dermatology

and ophthalmology. The segment also benefited from extension of lifespan for some of its legacy products such as Cital-PM6
solution, Nosic OD, and Ezetrol in Q1 FY2026. Going forward, the domestic market is expected to render stable revenue growth
for IRL in FY2026 and FY2027, supported by its strong market position in respective therapy segments.
Healthy geographic diversification – In FY2025 and Q1 FY2026, although the company witnessed a revenue decline in export
formulations, it was partially offset by revenue growth in domestic formulations. IRL derived around 90% of its sales revenue
in Q1 FY2026 from the formulation segment, with 53% of the segment’s revenues generated by domestic markets and the rest
from export markets. The company has a strong domestic presence, with its major brands positioned among the top five in
respective therapy segments. In terms of export markets, regulated markets such as the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia
and New Zealand generated 68% of its export formulation revenues, while the rest came from the emerging markets. Going
forward, the revenues are expected to remain diversified, with stable growth from domestic markets and an expected gradual
revival in revenues from key export markets.
Credit challenges
Pending resolution of OAI status from the USFDA for IRL’s Goa Plants II and III – IRL’s Goa Plants II and III were inspected by
USFDA in February 2023 and received their OAI status in June 2023. While IRL was working on the remediation, USFDA audited
the facility again in February 2024 and a warning letter was issued to the site in December 2024. IRL is working on remediating
the same, and its US revenues from the site were impacted to some extent due to the ongoing refurbishment. USFDA has given
approval for resumption of production for two lines of the four at the Goa Plant II recently. ICRA notes that the manufacturing
facility for Oral Solid Dosage (OSD) at Goa Plant I continues to remain Current Good Manufacturing Practice (CGMP) compliant
and supply to the US continues from this site. Going forward, any new Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA) filings from
the facility will be approved only when the OAI status is resolved and, hence, timely resolution of the same remains a key
monitorable.
Vulnerability to regulatory risks, raw material price and foreign exchange fluctuations – The company’s operations remain
exposed to regulatory risks due to increased scrutiny by the regulatory agencies and pricing controls in the domestic market.
ICRA notes that the company derives some revenues from products under the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM) but
draws comfort from the fact that the same has not materially impacted its profit margins. Nevertheless, any adverse changes
in Government price policies could lead to pricing pressures and affect the company’s domestic formulations business. IRL’s
profitability is also vulnerable to fluctuations in raw material, packaging and freight costs and their impact on margins will
remain a key monitorable. The company’s margins also remain vulnerable to foreign exchange fluctuations due to its overseas
operations and foreign currency borrowings despite hedging through forward contracts. ICRA notes that IRL capitalises
development expenditures for ANDAs/Drug Master Files (DMFs)/dossiers and any higher-than-expected price erosion or
lower-than-expected returns, exposes the company to the risk of impairment of intangibles.

operations and foreign currency borrowings despite hedging through forward contracts. ICRA notes that IRL capitalises
development expenditures for ANDAs/Drug Master Files (DMFs)/dossiers and any higher-than-expected price erosion or
lower-than-expected returns, exposes the company to the risk of impairment of intangibles.
Increasing working capital intensity of operations – The company’s working capital intensity was moderately high at 37.7% in
FY2025 and 34.0% in FY2024. For domestic sales, it typically offers a credit period of 7–90 days and for export sales, debtor
days range from 30–120 days. The company’s revenue from export markets (primarily in formulations) are working capital
intensive and resulted in a moderate rise in inventory days. IRL encountered regulatory issues during FY2018-FY2019, leading
to stretched payable days in FY2019. However, after the resolution of these issues and with improving cash accruals, IRL
substantially reduced its creditor days. Consequently, the working capital intensity has increased since then. Going forward,
as the company continues to focus on export markets, its working capital intensity is likely to remain in line with recent trends.
Sizeable debt-funded capex – While the company’s total debt level has reduced marginally to around Rs. 952 crore as on June
30, 2025 over Rs. 994 crore as on March 31, 2025 it remains elevated compared to Rs. 672 crore as on March 31, 2024. The
increase was primarily driven by the ongoing capex for refurbishing manufacturing plants in Goa and Baddi, and fast-tracked
debt-funded capex in its wholly-owned subsidiary, Warren Remedies Limited, to establish facilities for toothpaste and API
manufacturing. Overall, the company availed additional debt of about Rs. 264.3 crore in FY2025.
The company has funded its capex requirements with a mix of debt and internal accruals, with the debt component being 75-
78%. Consequently, the Total debt/OPBDITA increased to 10.0 times as on March 31, 2025 from 2.8 times as on March 31,

interest coverage ratio declining to 1.5 times in FY2025 from 6.4 times in FY2024. The interest coverage declined further to 0.7
times in Q1 FY2026 due to elevated interest; although interest costs included mark-to-market losses of around Rs. 7.4 crore,
which are notional in nature. The company is estimated to incur capex of Rs. 50-60 crore each in FY2026 and FY2027. Going
forward, stable performance in the domestic market supported by a revival in sales in key export markets and significant
expansion in operating margins remain crucial for the improvement in IRL’s debt metrics.
Environmental and Social Risks
Environmental considerations – The company does not face any major physical climate risk. However, it remains exposed to
tightening environmental regulations with regard to breach of waste and pollution norms, which can lead to an increase in
operating costs or capital investments. To address this, the company is dedicated to minimising its environmental footprint by
continuously improving its operations, reducing its energy consumption, and managing its waste and emissions responsibly.
IRL has recently installed solar power plants at two of its facilities and is planning to install more at other locations.
Social considerations – The industry faces social risks related to product safety and the associated litigation risks, access to
qualified personnel for R&D and process engineering and maintenance of high manufacturing compliance standards. Further,
Government intervention related to price caps/control also remains a social risk faced by entities in the pharmaceutical
industry. The company is committed to promoting the health and safety of its employees by providing a safe work
environment, supporting a culture of wellness, and investing in training and development. The company also supports local
initiatives, engages in philanthropic activities and partners with organisations that share its commitment to sustainability and
social responsibility.
Liquidity position: Adequate
The company’s liquidity position remains adequate with free cash and liquid investments of Rs. 15.76 crore as on June 30,
2025. The company’s working capital utilisation remains high, reflected by an average utilisation of 96.5% (against its average
drawing power (DP) of Rs. 346.8 crore) during the 12-month period ended in June 2025. IRL’s capex requirement for FY2026
are to be funded through internal accruals. It has debt servicing obligations of Rs. 68 crore for FY2026 and Rs. 139.4 crore for
FY2027. ICRA expects the company to meet its near-term repayment obligations through its accruals and existing cash
balances.
Rating sensitivities
Positive factors – The outlook may be revised to Stable in case the company demonstrates significant improvement in its
margins, leading to sustained improvement in its debt metrics, return indicators and liquidity position.
Negative factors – The rating may be downgraded if the company is unable to improve its revenues and margins materially by
scaling the additional capacities built over the last three years, leading to further weakening in the company’s overall financial
profile. Delays in resolution of existing regulatory non-compliance or any other regulatory non-compliance, thereby impacting
its product launches and, thus, revenues and profitability, would also be a negative rating trigger.

About the company
IRL was established by Mr. Govind Ramnath Kare in 1945 as Indo Continental Trading Company. It was involved in importing
pharmaceutical formulations from Europe and selling them in India. In 1963, the current Chairman and Managing Director,
Mr. Suresh G. Kare took over.
At present, IRL manufactures and markets branded formulations, APIs and contract research and manufacturing services
(CRAMS), with a strong presence in domestic formulations, which generated 53% of its total revenues in Q1 FY2026. In the
domestic business, the company has a prominent presence in the anti-infective, respiratory, gastrointestinal and dental
segments, with its major brands positioned among the top five in their respective categories. Export formulations comprised
36% of IRL’s revenues in Q1 FY2026, while APIs formed 10%, with the rest generated by contract research and analytics
divisions.
IRL’s formulation plants are in Goa (three plants), Waluj (Aurangabad, Maharashtra) and Baddi (Himachal Pradesh), while its
API plants are in Patalganga (Maharashtra) and Rabale (Navi Mumbai). The facilities have been approved by most major
regulatory authorities, including the USFDA and the UK-MHRA.

messages.content:
You are a senior credit analyst building a notebook of every fact that matters for deciding whether to grant a credit line to a borrower. You read a borrower's document pack one window at a time.

Write only facts that bear on the credit decision: repayment capacity, leverage, liquidity, cash flow, ratings, defaults, litigation and regulatory actions, auditor remarks, promoter holding and pledge, concentration, and the figures in the checklist below. Do not write boilerplate (meeting notices, e-voting and proxy mechanics), governance trivia (committee membership, attendance, meeting counts, policy lists), CSR and ESG programmes, awards, product marketing or generic industry narrative; when unsure whether a fact can change the decision, leave it out. Cover these categories exactly:
revenue, profitability, debt_leverage, liquidity, cash_flow, credit_history, ratings, stock,
ownership_governance, litigation_regulatory, industry_market, news, other.

Classify each entry's kind as one of:
- fact: a qualitative statement about the business, owners, or events.
- number: a figure, ratio, amount, date, or other measured quantity.
- concern: a risk, weakness, breach, or open question a credit officer should notice.

Give importance on this scale, and be stingy:
1 = boilerplate.
2 = minor detail.
3 = useful context (the default; most entries).
4 = only for a topic the bank's credit policy names: external ratings and outlook, litigation,
    auditor remarks or qualifications, promoter holding and pledge, regulatory actions
    (inspections, warning letters, penalties), defaults and overdue payments, and caution-list
    sectors (customer or supplier concentration, stressed sectors).
Never give 5: the program raises the facts that feed the bank's rules and scores itself.
Rate 4 only when the entry is about one of those topics; at most a fifth of your entries.

Rules:
- Cite only chunk ids that appear in the new chunks shown to you, in square brackets,
  such as D1:p12:c3. Never invent a chunk id.
- Prefer numbers with their period and unit (for example "Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in
  FY25"), and keep restatements separate when the period or basis changes.
- If a new entry restates or replaces an earlier notebook entry, set supersedes to that
  earlier entry's id.
- Write each statement as one self-contained sentence that can be verified against the
  cited chunks. Do not speculate beyond the document.
- Stay literal. Do not add comparisons ("exceeding", "higher than", "in line with"), causal
  qualifiers ("due to", "because", "driven by") or evaluations unless those exact words are in
  the cited text. Keep the text's own subject: never swap it for a related one (a "warning
  letter" is not an "OAI status"; a subsidiary is not the group).
- Always record rating actions, the outlook and its rationale, upgrade and downgrade triggers
  ("rating may be downgraded if ..."), and each rating-history row (as "rating was X on <date>;
  Y on <date>"), even if they repeat what an earlier document already said.
- Use the source's own metric names: never rename revenue as operating income or operating
  income as revenue, and never swap one metric for a related one.
- Every entry must carry at least one chunk id from the new chunks. Never omit the chunk id.
- Never write meta-commentary about the document or the passages ("the passages do not
  mention...", "no information is available"). If a window has nothing to record, return
  no entries.
- Return only the new entries for this window, not the entries already in the notebook.

Reply format: minified JSON on one line, no indentation, no Markdown fences, using the short keys of the schema (s statement, c chunk_ids, cat category, k kind, i importance, sup supersedes; for records m metric, v value, u unit, p period, sc scope, q qualifier, pv previous_value, pp previous_period). Omit keys whose value is the default (empty or null). Example:
{"entries":[{"s":"Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in FY25.","c":["D1:p12:c3"],"cat":"revenue","k":"number","i":4}],"records":[]}

Credit-policy checklist (Demo Bank of India — Corporate and SME Credit Policy (Working Capital and Term Credit)):
- Operating profit before depreciation, interest and tax, excluding other income
- Gross finance cost for the year
- Total borrowings (short and long term, including current maturities and leases)
- Shareholders' equity (net worth) at year end
- Total current assets at year end
- Total current liabilities at year end
- Revenue from operations, latest audited year
- Revenue from operations, previous audited year
- Financial Strength Score computed under policy section 10.1
- Internal Risk Grade computed under policy section 10.2
- Total borrowings less cash, bank balances and liquid investments, latest audited year: write its components (total borrowings, lease liabilities, cash and bank balances, liquid investments)
- Cash flow available for debt service: EBITDA less cash taxes paid: write its components (ebitda, cash taxes paid)
- Interest paid plus scheduled principal repayments in the year: write its components (interest paid, scheduled principal repayments)
- Tangible net worth at year end: write its components (total_equity, intangible assets)
- Rules tested: Net debt / EBITDA at most 4.5x; Interest coverage at least 2.5x; DSCR at least 1.25x; Current ratio at least 1.10x; Total debt / equity at most 3.0x; Revenue trend not below -10%; Tangible net worth positive; External rating at least BBB-; No default flag; Fewer than two major red flags; No major red flag; Proposed exposure within the maximum exposure; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 7; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 5; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 3
- Regulatory actions: warning letters, adverse inspections, licence suspensions, penalties (any regulator)
- External rating grade, outlook, watch status and rating history, the agency's metrics (interest coverage, DSCR) and rationale
- Auditor: qualifications, emphasis of matter, going-concern doubts (also on investees)
- Defaults: delays in repayment, CARO statements on dues, NPA or SMA classification
- Asset sales, monetisation, divestments and acquisitions
- Working capital: intensity, debtor and inventory days
- Latest quarter or half-year results: income, profit, margins

Rationale
The reaffirmation of the ratings and continuation of the Negative outlook on the long-term rating reflect Indoco Remedies
Limited’s (IRL/the company) elevated debt levels, weak debt-protection metrics and moderately high working capital intensity,
despite the recovery in its operating performance in FY2026. The ratings remain constrained by the continued regulatory
overhang at its Goa Plant II and uncertainty regarding the pace and sustainability of improvement in profitability, cash accruals
and leverage. The continued investments in the over-the-counter (OTC) oral care business under Warren Remedies Private
Limited have also constrained the company’s consolidated profitability in FY2026. While the completion of major plant
modifications under the Master Manufacturing Plan (MMP) and the liquidity infusion through recent asset monetisation
initiatives provide some comfort, a sustained improvement in operating performance and its translation into stronger cash
accruals, improvement in debt protection metrics and meaningful deleveraging remain to be demonstrated.
The company witnessed revenue growth of 10.8% to Rs. 1,845.3 crore in FY2026, supported by the recovery in export
formulations, healthy growth in the Active Pharmaceutical Ingredient (API) business and improved revenues from Warren
Remedies Private Limited. Export formulation revenues grew by 28.7% during the year, driven by growth of 14.4% in regulated
markets and 65.5% in non-regulated markets. The recovery in export formulations was also supported by the partial
resumption of operations at Goa Plant II after the United States Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) permitted the company
to restart production on two of its four production lines by July 2025. The operational lines enabled supplies of select injectable
and ophthalmic products, in turn supporting recovery in margins to an extent. However, IRL’s margins and earnings remain far
below previous levels.

The recovery continued in Q1 FY2027, with operating income rising by 6.0% YoY to Rs. 467.5 crore, supported by growth in the
US and API businesses.
The operating margin improved to 7.7% in FY2026 from 6.0% in FY2025, supported by the recovery in export sales and cost-
optimisation measures implemented under the MMP. The MMP enabled larger batch sizes, increased automation and reduced
manual intervention, thereby improving productivity and lowering per-unit manufacturing and testing costs. Workforce
rationalisation and other efficiencies under the MMP, is expected to generate annual savings of Rs. 14-15 crore. The
improvement continued in Q1 FY2027, with the operating margin growing to 8.8% from 4.0% in Q1 FY2026, supported by the
recovery in export sales and operating efficiencies from the MMP. However, the extent and sustainability of further margin
improvement remains to be seen, given elevated raw material costs amid geopolitical uncertainties, suboptimal utilisation of
Goa Plant II, and continued advertising and brand building expenditure at Warren Remedies Private Limited.
ICRA notes that the company has undertaken asset monetisation and working capital management initiatives to improve
liquidity. IRL received around Rs. 100 crore from the monetisation of its ophthalmic business and a cash inflow of around Rs.
64 crore from the sale of a land parcel in Mumbai in H1 FY2027. These proceeds, along with improved collections and scheduled
repayments, supported a reduction in consolidated debt in the recent months. However, the liquidity position remains
sensitive to the company’s ability to sustain operating cash flows amid a rising raw material price environment and contain its
working capital borrowings.
IRL’s financial risk profile remains constrained by elevated leverage and weak coverage indicators. Total debt stood at
Rs. 1,084.2 crore as on March 31, 2026, while total debt/OPBDITA remained high at 7.6 times. Interest coverage and DSCR
were weak at 1.2 times and 0.7 times, respectively, in FY2026. Further, working capital intensity remained moderately high at
34.6%, reflecting longer receivable cycles in export markets and sizeable inventory requirements. Although the anticipated
recovery in earnings and scheduled debt repayments could support a gradual improvement in credit metrics, the pace and
sustainability of deleveraging remain key monitorables.
The ratings also remain exposed to regulatory risks associated with the pending resolution of the USFDA warning letter for
Goa Plant II. The USFDA inspection conducted during August 27–September 4, 2026 resulted in seven Form 483 observations.
Timely and satisfactory resolution of the observations remains critical for removing the regulatory overhang, securing new
product approvals and improving capacity utilisation at the facility. Any delay in regulatory closure or fresh adverse regulatory
action could constrain production, product launches, exports and profitability.
The ratings continue to draw comfort from IRL’s established presence in the domestic formulations market, diversified
geographical footprint, strong brands across key therapeutic segments, experienced management and backward integrated
operations. Further, receipt of the USFDA Establishment Inspection Report (EIR) for IRL’s Patalganga API facility in December
2025 is expected to support its operating profile. However, sustained improvement in profitability, cash accruals, leverage and

Key rating drivers and their description
Credit strengths
Experienced promoter and management team – At present, the company’s operations are managed by Ms. Aditi Kare
Panandikar and Mr. Sundeep Bambolkar, both of whom have over 30 years of experience in the pharmaceutical industry,
supported by a professional management team.
Established brands in dental, respiratory, gastrointestinal and anti-infective therapies of domestic formulations market –
IRL has an established presence in the domestic formulations market, with wide therapeutic coverage across gastrointestinal,
respiratory, anti-infective, stomatological and vitamins/minerals/nutrients segments. The company’s major brands enjoy
leading positions in their respective sub-segments, with major brands positioned among the top five of the respective therapy
segments, including Cyclopam, Sensodent-K, Karvol Plus, Kidodent and Rexidin M, which held the leading position in their

business. However, IRL’s sizeable presence in mature acute-therapy molecules exposes it to intense competition, seasonal
demand volatility and limited pricing flexibility. Going forward, the domestic formulations business is expected to grow
supported by volume growth, improved retail availability, price increases and healthy contribution from new product launches,
continued traction in flagship brands and lifecycle extensions of established products such as Cital-PM6 Solution, Nosic OD and
Ezetrol.
Healthy geographic diversification – IRL benefits from a diversified geographical presence across domestic, regulated and non-
regulated markets. In FY2026, domestic and export formulations contributed 46.6% and 36.8%, respectively, to the overall
revenues. The export formulations business is further diversified across regulated markets, comprising Europe, the US, South
Africa, Australia and New Zealand, and semi-regulated markets spanning Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Commonwealth
of Independent States (CIS) countries. This diversified geographical presence partly mitigates concentration risks arising from
demand volatility, regulatory developments or supply disruptions in any single market. Going forward, the revenue profile is
expected to remain diversified, supported by stable growth in the domestic business and a gradual recovery across key export
markets following the normalisation of supplies and completion of major plant upgradation under the MMP.
Improved manufacturing efficiency following implementation of the MMP – The completion of major plant upgradation
under the MMP in FY2026 strengthened IRL’s manufacturing capabilities through equipment upgrades, product realignment,
increased automation, larger batch sizes and reduced manual intervention. Facilities have also been substantially automated,
resulting in lower manual intervention and manpower requirements, along with stronger process controls. Going forward,
larger batch sizes, automation and workforce rationalisation are expected to improve productivity, reduce per-unit
manufacturing and testing costs, and support operating leverage as export volumes and capacity utilisation improve.
Nevertheless, the full benefits remain dependent on the quantum of improvement in the revenues and margins the company
can achieve through the benefits accrued from the MMP.
Credit challenges
Pending resolution of OAI status from USFDA for IRL’s Goa Plants II and III – IRL’s Goa Plants II and III were inspected by
USFDA in February 2023 and received their Operating Agency Inspection (OAI) status in June 2023. While IRL was working on
the remediation, USFDA audited the facility again in February 2024 and a warning letter was issued to the site. All four
production lines were shut down in April 2024 for remediation and refurbishment, resulting in supply disruptions and
restricting approvals for new products linked to the facility. The USFDA subsequently permitted the resumption of
manufacturing on two of the four lines at Goa Plant II in July 2025, which supported the partial recovery of US revenues in
FY2026. ICRA notes that subsequently, a three-member USFDA team reinspected Goa Plant II during August 27–September 4,
2026, resulting in seven Form 483 observations. Timely and satisfactory resolution of the observations and receipt of the EIR
remain critical for resolving the regulatory overhang, securing new product approvals, ramping up the remaining production
lines and improving the utilisation and profitability of the facility. Any delay in regulatory closure or fresh adverse regulatory
action could constrain product approvals, exports and profitability.

Vulnerability to regulatory risks, raw material price and forex fluctuations – IRL’s operations remain exposed to regulatory
risks arising from heightened scrutiny by regulatory authorities across domestic and export markets. The domestic
formulations business to the tune of about 11%-13% is also subject to Government mandated pricing controls, as a portion of
the company’s product portfolio is covered under the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM). Although these controls
have not materially affected profitability in the past, any adverse revision in Government pricing policies could constrain pricing
flexibility and exert pressure on the domestic formulations business. The company’s profitability also remains vulnerable to
fluctuations in raw material, packaging and freight costs, with the impact on margins remaining a key monitorable. Further,
despite the use of forward contracts, IRL remains exposed to foreign exchange (forex) fluctuations arising from its overseas
operations and foreign currency borrowings. IRL also capitalises development expenditure incurred on Abbreviated New Drug
Applications (ANDAs), Drug Master Files and dossiers. Consequently, higher-than-anticipated price erosion, delays in
commercialisation or lower-than-expected returns from the related products could result in impairment of intangible assets.

Elevated working capital intensity of operations – IRL’s working capital intensity remained moderately high at 34.6% in
FY2026; although it moderated from 37.7% in FY2025 following improved inventory movement and the gradual normalisation
of operations. The company’s export formulations business remains working capital intensive owing to relatively long
receivable cycles, while sizeable inventory is maintained to manage procurement lead times and ensure continuity of
production. Nevertheless, inventory days declined to 124 days in FY2026 from 139 days in FY2025, reflecting improved product
movement and dispatches following the easing of plant-related disruptions. Creditor days increased to 198 days from 141 days
amid pressure on cash flows and delayed supplier payments. Subsequently, liquidity generated through asset monetisation
initiatives, along with improved collections, enabled the company to settle most creditors outstanding for more than 90 days
and reduce working capital borrowings. Going forward, working capital intensity is expected to remain moderately high as the
company continues to focus on export markets, with sustained improvement in collections and inventory management
remaining key monitorables.
Weak profitability and elevated debt levels constrain financial risk profile – IRL’s financial risk profile remains constrained by
subdued profitability, elevated debt levels and weak debt-protection metrics. Although the operating margin improved to 7.7%
in FY2026 from 6.0% in FY2025, it remained significantly below historical levels amid the suboptimal utilisation of Goa Plant II,
implementation of MMP, and continued losses at Warren Remedies Private Limited. Despite the improvement in operating
profit, the company’s net loss widened to Rs. 98.7 crore in FY2026 from Rs. 78.0 crore in FY2025, primarily because of elevated
depreciation and finance costs following the sizeable debt-funded capital expenditure (capex) incurred in the preceding years.
Warren Remedies also reported a higher loss before tax of Rs. 64.3 crore in FY2026 over Rs. 36.0 crore in FY2025, owing to
sustained advertising and brand-building expenditure, finance costs and depreciation associated with its new facilities, and
operating expenses at the API plant, where products remained under validation.
The company had undertaken sizeable capex in the preceding years towards capacity expansion, implementation of the MMP,
additional production lines at Goa Plant II, and the toothpaste and API manufacturing facilities of Warren Remedies. With the
completion of the major capacity expansion and plant upgradation projects by FY2026, the company does not envisage any
significant capex over the near term. The proposed expenditure in the current fiscal is expected to be restricted primarily to
essential maintenance, energy saving initiatives and boiler installations, which should limit incremental funding requirements.
Going forward, profitability is expected to improve gradually, supported by the recovery in margin accretive export sales,
higher capacity utilisation, larger batch sizes, automation, manpower rationalisation and better absorption of fixed overheads.
Environmental and social risks
Environmental considerations – The company is not exposed to any significant physical climate-related risks. However, it
remains susceptible to evolving and increasingly stringent environmental regulations, particularly with respect to waste
management and pollution control norms. Any non-compliance or tightening of such regulations could lead to higher operating
costs as well as increased costs for future capacity additions.
Social considerations – The company is exposed to elevated industry-wide social risks, primarily driven by stringent product
safety requirements and the associated risk of litigation.

Liquidity position: Adequate
The company’s liquidity position remains adequate with free cash and liquid investments of Rs. 26.2 crore as on March 31,
2026. The company’s working capital utilisation remains elevated, reflected by an average utilisation of 90.7% against its
drawing power (during the 12-month period ending in July 2026). IRL’s capex requirement over the near to medium term is to
be funded through internal accruals. It has debt servicing obligations of Rs. 145.8 crore for FY2027 and Rs. 145.3 crore for
FY2028. ICRA expects the company to meet its near-term repayment obligations through its accruals and existing cash balances
in addition to funds raised from the sale of its ophthalmic division and a land parcel in Mumbai in H1 FY2027.

Rating sensitivities
Positive factors – The outlook may be revised to Stable in case the company demonstrates significant improvement in its
margins, leading to sustained improvement in its debt metrics, return indicators and liquidity position.
Negative factors – The rating may be downgraded if the company is unable to improve its revenues and margins materially by
scaling the additional capacities built over the last three years, leading to further weakening in the company’s overall financial
profile. Delays in resolution of existing regulatory non-compliance or any other regulatory non-compliance, thereby impacting
its product launches and, thus, revenues and profitability, would also be a negative rating trigger.

About the company
Indoco Remedies Limited was established by Mr. Govind Ramnath Kare in 1947 as Indo Continental Trading
Company and was involved in imports of pharmaceutical formulations from Europe and their sales in India. In 1963,
the current Chairman, Mr. Suresh G. Kare took over. At present, IRL manufactures and markets branded
formulations and APIs, and is engaged in providing contract research and manufacturing services (CRAMS) with a
strong presence in domestic formulations, which contributed to around 44.3% of its total revenues in FY2026
(consolidated). In the domestic business, IRL has a prominent presence in the anti-infective, respiratory, gastro-
intestinal and dental segments.
The export formulations business comprised 39% of IRL’s revenues in FY2026 while APIs accounted for 9% in FY2026
with the balance derived from contract research and analytics. IRL’s formulations plants are located at Goa (three
plants), Waluj (Aurangabad, Maharashtra) and Baddi (Himachal Pradesh; two plants), while API units are located at
Patalganga (Maharashtra) and Rabale (Navi Mumbai). In FY2017, IRL acquired Micro Labs Limited’s solid oral dosage
manufacturing facility at Baddi, which is being utilised to manufacture formulations for the European and the UK
markets. Overall, IRL has 10 manufacturing facilities in India, six for finished dosages and four for APIs, supported
by an R&D centre, a Clinical Research Organization (CRO) and a Global Stability Centre. The company’s
manufacturing facilities are approved by various regulatory authorities including USFDA, UK-MHRA and TGA-
Australia. In FY2025, the company established a wholly-owned subsidiary, Warren Remedies Private Limited, to
enter the OTC segment.

messages.content:
You are a senior credit analyst building a notebook of every fact that matters for deciding whether to grant a credit line to a borrower. You read a borrower's document pack one window at a time.

Write only facts that bear on the credit decision: repayment capacity, leverage, liquidity, cash flow, ratings, defaults, litigation and regulatory actions, auditor remarks, promoter holding and pledge, concentration, and the figures in the checklist below. Do not write boilerplate (meeting notices, e-voting and proxy mechanics), governance trivia (committee membership, attendance, meeting counts, policy lists), CSR and ESG programmes, awards, product marketing or generic industry narrative; when unsure whether a fact can change the decision, leave it out. Cover these categories exactly:
revenue, profitability, debt_leverage, liquidity, cash_flow, credit_history, ratings, stock,
ownership_governance, litigation_regulatory, industry_market, news, other.

Classify each entry's kind as one of:
- fact: a qualitative statement about the business, owners, or events.
- number: a figure, ratio, amount, date, or other measured quantity.
- concern: a risk, weakness, breach, or open question a credit officer should notice.

Give importance on this scale, and be stingy:
1 = boilerplate.
2 = minor detail.
3 = useful context (the default; most entries).
4 = only for a topic the bank's credit policy names: external ratings and outlook, litigation,
    auditor remarks or qualifications, promoter holding and pledge, regulatory actions
    (inspections, warning letters, penalties), defaults and overdue payments, and caution-list
    sectors (customer or supplier concentration, stressed sectors).
Never give 5: the program raises the facts that feed the bank's rules and scores itself.
Rate 4 only when the entry is about one of those topics; at most a fifth of your entries.

Rules:
- Cite only chunk ids that appear in the new chunks shown to you, in square brackets,
  such as D1:p12:c3. Never invent a chunk id.
- Prefer numbers with their period and unit (for example "Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in
  FY25"), and keep restatements separate when the period or basis changes.
- If a new entry restates or replaces an earlier notebook entry, set supersedes to that
  earlier entry's id.
- Write each statement as one self-contained sentence that can be verified against the
  cited chunks. Do not speculate beyond the document.
- Stay literal. Do not add comparisons ("exceeding", "higher than", "in line with"), causal
  qualifiers ("due to", "because", "driven by") or evaluations unless those exact words are in
  the cited text. Keep the text's own subject: never swap it for a related one (a "warning
  letter" is not an "OAI status"; a subsidiary is not the group).
- Always record rating actions, the outlook and its rationale, upgrade and downgrade triggers
  ("rating may be downgraded if ..."), and each rating-history row (as "rating was X on <date>;
  Y on <date>"), even if they repeat what an earlier document already said.
- Use the source's own metric names: never rename revenue as operating income or operating
  income as revenue, and never swap one metric for a related one.
- Every entry must carry at least one chunk id from the new chunks. Never omit the chunk id.
- Never write meta-commentary about the document or the passages ("the passages do not
  mention...", "no information is available"). If a window has nothing to record, return
  no entries.
- Return only the new entries for this window, not the entries already in the notebook.

Reply format: minified JSON on one line, no indentation, no Markdown fences, using the short keys of the schema (s statement, c chunk_ids, cat category, k kind, i importance, sup supersedes; for records m metric, v value, u unit, p period, sc scope, q qualifier, pv previous_value, pp previous_period). Omit keys whose value is the default (empty or null). Example:
{"entries":[{"s":"Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in FY25.","c":["D1:p12:c3"],"cat":"revenue","k":"number","i":4}],"records":[]}

Credit-policy checklist (Demo Bank of India — Corporate and SME Credit Policy (Working Capital and Term Credit)):
- Operating profit before depreciation, interest and tax, excluding other income
- Gross finance cost for the year
- Total borrowings (short and long term, including current maturities and leases)
- Shareholders' equity (net worth) at year end
- Total current assets at year end
- Total current liabilities at year end
- Revenue from operations, latest audited year
- Revenue from operations, previous audited year
- Financial Strength Score computed under policy section 10.1
- Internal Risk Grade computed under policy section 10.2
- Total borrowings less cash, bank balances and liquid investments, latest audited year: write its components (total borrowings, lease liabilities, cash and bank balances, liquid investments)
- Cash flow available for debt service: EBITDA less cash taxes paid: write its components (ebitda, cash taxes paid)
- Interest paid plus scheduled principal repayments in the year: write its components (interest paid, scheduled principal repayments)
- Tangible net worth at year end: write its components (total_equity, intangible assets)
- Rules tested: Net debt / EBITDA at most 4.5x; Interest coverage at least 2.5x; DSCR at least 1.25x; Current ratio at least 1.10x; Total debt / equity at most 3.0x; Revenue trend not below -10%; Tangible net worth positive; External rating at least BBB-; No default flag; Fewer than two major red flags; No major red flag; Proposed exposure within the maximum exposure; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 7; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 5; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 3
- Regulatory actions: warning letters, adverse inspections, licence suspensions, penalties (any regulator)
- External rating grade, outlook, watch status and rating history, the agency's metrics (interest coverage, DSCR) and rationale
- Auditor: qualifications, emphasis of matter, going-concern doubts (also on investees)
- Defaults: delays in repayment, CARO statements on dues, NPA or SMA classification
- Asset sales, monetisation, divestments and acquisitions
- Working capital: intensity, debtor and inventory days
- Latest quarter or half-year results: income, profit, margins
- Red-flag and default evidence: adverse opinion, auditor resign, default, disclaimer, forensic, Form 483, fraud, going concern, IBC, insolvency, litigation, non-performing, NPA, OAI, one-time settlement, OTS, overdue, pledge, promoter loan, qualification, qualified, regulatory proceeding, related party, related-party, resignation, SMA, warning letter, wilful

messages.content:
You are a senior credit analyst building a notebook of every fact that matters for deciding whether to grant a credit line to a borrower. You read a borrower's document pack one window at a time.

Write only facts that bear on the credit decision: repayment capacity, leverage, liquidity, cash flow, ratings, defaults, litigation and regulatory actions, auditor remarks, promoter holding and pledge, concentration, and the figures in the checklist below. Do not write boilerplate (meeting notices, e-voting and proxy mechanics), governance trivia (committee membership, attendance, meeting counts, policy lists), CSR and ESG programmes, awards, product marketing or generic industry narrative; when unsure whether a fact can change the decision, leave it out. Cover these categories exactly:
revenue, profitability, debt_leverage, liquidity, cash_flow, credit_history, ratings, stock,
ownership_governance, litigation_regulatory, industry_market, news, other.

Classify each entry's kind as one of:
- fact: a qualitative statement about the business, owners, or events.
- number: a figure, ratio, amount, date, or other measured quantity.
- concern: a risk, weakness, breach, or open question a credit officer should notice.

Give importance on this scale, and be stingy:
1 = boilerplate.
2 = minor detail.
3 = useful context (the default; most entries).
4 = only for a topic the bank's credit policy names: external ratings and outlook, litigation,
    auditor remarks or qualifications, promoter holding and pledge, regulatory actions
    (inspections, warning letters, penalties), defaults and overdue payments, and caution-list
    sectors (customer or supplier concentration, stressed sectors).
Never give 5: the program raises the facts that feed the bank's rules and scores itself.
Rate 4 only when the entry is about one of those topics; at most a fifth of your entries.

Rules:
- Cite only chunk ids that appear in the new chunks shown to you, in square brackets,
  such as D1:p12:c3. Never invent a chunk id.
- Prefer numbers with their period and unit (for example "Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in
  FY25"), and keep restatements separate when the period or basis changes.
- If a new entry restates or replaces an earlier notebook entry, set supersedes to that
  earlier entry's id.
- Write each statement as one self-contained sentence that can be verified against the
  cited chunks. Do not speculate beyond the document.
- Stay literal. Do not add comparisons ("exceeding", "higher than", "in line with"), causal
  qualifiers ("due to", "because", "driven by") or evaluations unless those exact words are in
  the cited text. Keep the text's own subject: never swap it for a related one (a "warning
  letter" is not an "OAI status"; a subsidiary is not the group).
- Always record rating actions, the outlook and its rationale, upgrade and downgrade triggers
  ("rating may be downgraded if ..."), and each rating-history row (as "rating was X on <date>;
  Y on <date>"), even if they repeat what an earlier document already said.
- Use the source's own metric names: never rename revenue as operating income or operating
  income as revenue, and never swap one metric for a related one.
- Every entry must carry at least one chunk id from the new chunks. Never omit the chunk id.
- Never write meta-commentary about the document or the passages ("the passages do not
  mention...", "no information is available"). If a window has nothing to record, return
  no entries.
- Return only the new entries for this window, not the entries already in the notebook.

Reply format: minified JSON on one line, no indentation, no Markdown fences, using the short keys of the schema (s statement, c chunk_ids, cat category, k kind, i importance, sup supersedes; for records m metric, v value, u unit, p period, sc scope, q qualifier, pv previous_value, pp previous_period). Omit keys whose value is the default (empty or null). Example:
{"entries":[{"s":"Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in FY25.","c":["D1:p12:c3"],"cat":"revenue","k":"number","i":4}],"records":[]}

Credit-policy checklist (Demo Bank of India — Corporate and SME Credit Policy (Working Capital and Term Credit)):
- Operating profit before depreciation, interest and tax, excluding other income
- Gross finance cost for the year
- Total borrowings (short and long term, including current maturities and leases)
- Shareholders' equity (net worth) at year end
- Total current assets at year end
- Total current liabilities at year end
- Revenue from operations, latest audited year
- Revenue from operations, previous audited year
- Financial Strength Score computed under policy section 10.1
- Internal Risk Grade computed under policy section 10.2
- Total borrowings less cash, bank balances and liquid investments, latest audited year: write its components (total borrowings, lease liabilities, cash and bank balances, liquid investments)
- Cash flow available for debt service: EBITDA less cash taxes paid: write its components (ebitda, cash taxes paid)
- Interest paid plus scheduled principal repayments in the year: write its components (interest paid, scheduled principal repayments)
- Tangible net worth at year end: write its components (total_equity, intangible assets)
- Rules tested: Net debt / EBITDA at most 4.5x; Interest coverage at least 2.5x; DSCR at least 1.25x; Current ratio at least 1.10x; Total debt / equity at most 3.0x; Revenue trend not below -10%; Tangible net worth positive; External rating at least BBB-; No default flag; Fewer than two major red flags; No major red flag; Proposed exposure within the maximum exposure; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 7; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 5; Internal Risk Grade 1 to 3
- Regulatory actions: warning letters, adverse inspections, licence suspensions, penalties (any regulator)
- External rating grade, outlook, watch status and rating history, the agency's metrics (interest coverage, DSCR) and rationale
- Auditor: qualifications, emphasis of matter, going-concern doubts (also on investees)
- Defaults: delays in repayment, CARO statements on dues, NPA or SMA classification
- Asset sales, monetisation, divestments and acquisitions
- Working capital: intensity, debtor and inventory days
- Latest quarter or half-year results: income, profit, margins
- Red-flag and default evidence: adverse opinion, auditor resign, default, disclaimer, forensic, Form 483, fraud, going concern, IBC, insolvency, litigation, non-performing, NPA, OAI, one-time settlement, OTS, overdue, pledge, promoter loan, qualification, qualified, regulatory proceeding, related party, related-party, resignation, SMA, warning letter, wilful

messages.content:
You are a senior credit analyst building a notebook of every fact that matters for deciding whether to grant a credit line to a borrower. You read a borrower's document pack one window at a time.

Write only facts that bear on the credit decision: repayment capacity, leverage, liquidity, cash flow, ratings, defaults, litigation and regulatory actions, auditor remarks, promoter holding and pledge, concentration, and the figures in the checklist below. Do not write boilerplate (meeting notices, e-voting and proxy mechanics), governance trivia (committee membership, attendance, meeting counts, policy lists), CSR and ESG programmes, awards, product marketing or generic industry narrative; when unsure whether a fact can change the decision, leave it out. Cover these categories exactly:
revenue, profitability, debt_leverage, liquidity, cash_flow, credit_history, ratings, stock,
ownership_governance, litigation_regulatory, industry_market, news, other.

Classify each entry's kind as one of:
- fact: a qualitative statement about the business, owners, or events.
- number: a figure, ratio, amount, date, or other measured quantity.
- concern: a risk, weakness, breach, or open question a credit officer should notice.

Give importance on this scale, and be stingy:
1 = boilerplate.
2 = minor detail.
3 = useful context (the default; most entries).
4 = only for a topic the bank's credit policy names: external ratings and outlook, litigation,
    auditor remarks or qualifications, promoter holding and pledge, regulatory actions
    (inspections, warning letters, penalties), defaults and overdue payments, and caution-list
    sectors (customer or supplier concentration, stressed sectors).
Never give 5: the program raises the facts that feed the bank's rules and scores itself.
Rate 4 only when the entry is about one of those topics; at most a fifth of your entries.

Rules:
- Cite only chunk ids that appear in the new chunks shown to you, in square brackets,
  such as D1:p12:c3. Never invent a chunk id.
- Prefer numbers with their period and unit (for example "Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in
  FY25"), and keep restatements separate when the period or basis changes.
- If a new entry restates or replaces an earlier notebook entry, set supersedes to that
  earlier entry's id.
- Write each statement as one self-contained sentence that can be verified against the
  cited chunks. Do not speculate beyond the document.
- Stay literal. Do not add comparisons ("exceeding", "higher than", "in line with"), causal
  qualifiers ("due to", "because", "driven by") or evaluations unless those exact words are in
  the cited text. Keep the text's own subject: never swap it for a related one (a "warning
  letter" is not an "OAI status"; a subsidiary is not the group).
- Always record rating actions, the outlook and its rationale, upgrade and downgrade triggers
  ("rating may be downgraded if ..."), and each rating-history row (as "rating was X on <date>;
  Y on <date>"), even if they repeat what an earlier document already said.
- Use the source's own metric names: never rename revenue as operating income or operating
  income as revenue, and never swap one metric for a related one.
- Every entry must carry at least one chunk id from the new chunks. Never omit the chunk id.
- Never write meta-commentary about the document or the passages ("the passages do not
  mention...", "no information is available"). If a window has nothing to record, return
  no entries.
- Return only the new entries for this window, not the entries already in the notebook.

Reply format: minified JSON on one line, no indentation, no Markdown fences, using the short keys of the schema (s statement, c chunk_ids, cat category, k kind, i importance, sup supersedes; for records m metric, v value, u unit, p period, sc scope, q qualifier, pv previous_value, pp previous_period). Omit keys whose value is the default (empty or null). Example:
{"entries":[{"s":"Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in FY25.","c":["D1:p12:c3"],"cat":"revenue","k":"number","i":4}],"records":[]}

Credit-policy checklist (Demo Bank of India — Corporate and SME Credit Policy (Working Capital and Term Credit)):
- Operating profit before depreciation, interest and tax, excluding other income
- Gross finance cost for the year
- Total borrowings (short and long term, including current maturities and leases)
- Shareholders' equity (net worth) at year end
- Total current assets at year end
- Total current liabilities at year end
- Revenue from operations, latest audited year
- Revenue from operations, previous audited year
- Financial Strength Score computed under policy section 10.1
- Internal Risk Grade computed under policy section 10.2
- Total borrowings less cash, bank balances and liquid investments, latest audited year: write its components (total borrowings, lease liabilities, cash and bank balances, liquid investments)

Report on the Internal Financial Controls under Clause (i) of subsection 3 of Section 143 of the Companies
Act, 2013 (the “Act”)
Opinion
We have audited the internal financial controls with reference to standalone financial statements of
INDOCO REMEDIES LIMITED (the “Company”) as of March 31, 2026 in conjunction with our audit of
the standalone financial statements of the Company for the year ended on that date.
In our opinion, to the best of our information and according to the explanations given to us, the Company
has, in all material respects, an adequate internal financial controls system with reference to standalone
financial statements and such internal financial controls with reference to standalone financial statements
were operating effectively as at March 31, 2026, based on the criteria for internal financial control over
financial reporting established by the Company considering the essential components of internal control
stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting issued by
the ICAI.
Managements’ Responsibility for Internal Financial Controls
The Management of the Company is responsible for establishing and maintaining internal financial controls
with reference to standalone financial statements based on the internal control over financial reporting
criteria established by the Company considering the essential components of internal control stated in the
Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting issued by the Institute of
Chartered Accountants of India (the “ICAI”). These responsibilities include the design, implementation and
maintenance of adequate internal financial controls that were operating effectively for ensuring the orderly
and efficient conduct of its business, including adherence to company’s policies, the safeguarding of its
assets, the prevention and detection of frauds and errors, the accuracy and completeness of the accounting
records, and the timely preparation of reliable financial information, as required under the Act.
Auditors’ Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company’s internal financial controls with reference
to standalone financial statements based on our audit. We conducted our audit in accordance with the
Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting (the “Guidance Note”)
issued by the ICAI and the Standards on Auditing prescribed under Section 143(10) of the Act, to the extent
applicable to an audit of internal financial controls with reference to standalone financial statements.
Those Standards and the Guidance Note require that we comply with ethical requirements and plan and
perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether adequate internal financial controls with
reference to standalone financial statements was established and maintained and if such controls operated
effectively in all material respects.
Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the adequacy of the internal
financial controls with reference to standalone financial statements and their operating effectiveness.
Our audit of internal financial controls with reference to standalone financial statements included
obtaining an understanding of internal financial controls with reference to financial statements, assessing
the risk that a material weakness exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness
A N N U A L R E P O R T 2 0 2 5 - 2 0 2 6
184

[D1:p186:c0]
of internal control based on the assessed risk. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgement,
including the assessment of the risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to
fraud or error.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained, is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for
our audit opinion on the Company’s internal financial controls with reference to standalone financial
statements.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting with reference to standalone financial
statements
A company’s internal financial control over financial reporting is a process designed to provide
reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of standalone
financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A
company’s internal financial control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures that
1)
pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the
transactions and dispositions of the assets of the Company;
2)
provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of
standalone financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and
that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations
of management and directors of the company; and
3)
provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition,
use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material effect on the standalone
financial statements.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial Reporting with reference to financial
statements.
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial controls over financial reporting, including the
possibility of collusion or improper management override of controls, material misstatements due to error
or fraud may occur and not be detected. Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal financial
controls over financial reporting to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal financial control
over financial reporting may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of
185
compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.

You are a senior credit analyst building a notebook of every fact that matters for deciding whether to grant a credit line to a borrower. You read a borrower's document pack one window at a time.

Write only facts that bear on the credit decision: repayment capacity, leverage, liquidity, cash flow, ratings, defaults, litigation and regulatory actions, auditor remarks, promoter holding and pledge, concentration, and the figures in the checklist below. Do not write boilerplate (meeting notices, e-voting and proxy mechanics), governance trivia (committee membership, attendance, meeting counts, policy lists), CSR and ESG programmes, awards, product marketing or generic industry narrative; when unsure whether a fact can change the decision, leave it out. Cover these categories exactly:
revenue, profitability, debt_leverage, liquidity, cash_flow, credit_history, ratings, stock,
ownership_governance, litigation_regulatory, industry_market, news, other.

Classify each entry's kind as one of:
- fact: a qualitative statement about the business, owners, or events.
- number: a figure, ratio, amount, date, or other measured quantity.
- concern: a risk, weakness, breach, or open question a credit officer should notice.

Give importance on this scale, and be stingy:
1 = boilerplate.
2 = minor detail.
3 = useful context (the default; most entries).
4 = only for a topic the bank's credit policy names: external ratings and outlook, litigation,
    auditor remarks or qualifications, promoter holding and pledge, regulatory actions
    (inspections, warning letters, penalties), defaults and overdue payments, and caution-list
    sectors (customer or supplier concentration, stressed sectors).
Never give 5: the program raises the facts that feed the bank's rules and scores itself.
Rate 4 only when the entry is about one of those topics; at most a fifth of your entries.

Rules:
- Cite only chunk ids that appear in the new chunks shown to you, in square brackets,
  such as D1:p12:c3. Never invent a chunk id.
- Prefer numbers with their period and unit (for example "Revenue was INR 931.2 crore in
  FY25"), and keep restatements separate when the period or basis changes.
- If a new entry restates or replaces an earlier notebook entry, set supersedes to that
  earlier entry's id.
- Write each statement as one self-contained sentence that can be verified against the
  cited chunks. Do not speculate beyond the document.
- Stay literal. Do not add comparisons ("exceeding", "higher than", "in line with"), causal
  qualifiers ("due to", "because", "driven by") or evaluations unless those exact words are in
  the cited text. Keep the text's own subject: never swap it for a related one (a "warning
  letter" is not an "OAI status"; a subsidiary is not the group).
- Always record rating actions, the outlook and its rationale, upgrade and downgrade triggers
  ("rating may be downgraded if ..."), and each rating-history row (as "rating was X on <date>;
  Y on <date>"), even if they repeat what an earlier document already said.
- Use the source's own metric names: never rename revenue as operating income or operating

- Never write meta-commentary about the document or the passages ("the passages do not
  mention...", "no information is available"). If a window has nothing to record, return
  no entries.

- Gross finance cost for the year

criteria of independence as prescribed under Section 149(6) of the Act read with Regulation 16(1)(b) of
